newsitem.title: UK: Hume urges British reply to N.Irish peace bid.
newsitem.headline: Hume urges British reply to N.Irish peace bid.

text.p: A Northern Ireland Catholic leader on Sunday urged Britain to step up efforts for an IRA truce after Britain told the guerrilla group "the ball is now in your court."

Catholic nationalist John Hume, in an optimistic view on prospects for peace, said a truce might be on the cards if Major agreed to a formula for serious all-party talks involving the Irish Republican Army's political arm Sinn Fein.

He said Major would help to dispel republican distrust if he supported peace proposals that Hume had put to him after meeting with Sinn Fein leader Gerry Adams a month ago. "The objective of that dialogue was an unequivocal restoration of the IRA's ceasefire," Hume, head of the moderately Irish nationalist Social Democratic and Labour Party (SDLP), told Irish radio. "I believe that that is very possible if there is a statement from the British government making very clear that the talks process is a serious process."

The IRA resumed its bombing campaign in February, ending a 17-month ceasefire in a battle to end British rule over Northern Ireland. Majority Protestants and minority Catholics are divided over the future of British rule.

Police prevented members of the pro-British Protestant "Orange Order" institution from marching in the largely pro-Irish Catholic village of Dunloy in County Antrim north of Belfast on Sunday after Catholic residents held a counter-demonstration.
A police spokesman said the ban was made "to prevent serious disorder".
Hume's predictions of an early IRA truce found little echo with Protestant Unionist politicians.
David Trimble, leader of the Ulster Unionist Party (UUP) which speaks for most of the 60 per cent Protestants, said he saw no evidence of an early IRA ceasefire.
"The current talk of peace is merely camouflage behind which their preparations for violence advance," he told BBC television.

Britain signalled no change in its policy of a truce as a prerequisite for Sinn Fein entry to talks. Britain's junior Northern Ireland Minister Michael Ancram told the guerrillas: "The ball is now in your court."
He added: "They must demonstrate openly and convincingly that this time their ceasefire would be for real and would be for good."
